summary.text: Take \(N=2^{14}\cdot4409\cdot458009\); primality and coprimality of the factors, together with multiplicativity, give \(\sigma(N)=32767\cdot4410\cdot458010\) and \(\sum_{d\mid N}\sigma(d)=65519\cdot4411\cdot458011\). Thus \(2\sigma(N)-\sum_{d\mid N}\sigma(d)=1\), although \(N\ne1,12\), furnishing the counterexample.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\sigma(n)=\sum_{e\mid n}e\) denote the sum of the positive divisors of \(n\). The deficiency of a positive integer \(d\) is
\[
\delta(d)=2d-\sigma(d),
\]
so the sequence in question is
\[
a(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\delta(d)=\sum_{d\mid n}\bigl(2d-\sigma(d)\bigr).
\]
We will exhibit a positive integer other than \(1\) and \(12\) for which this sum is \(1\).

Define the auxiliary divisor sum
\[
Y(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d).
\]
Since \(\sum_{d\mid n}d=\sigma(n)\), rearranging the definition of \(a(n)\) gives the fundamental identity
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(n)
 &=2\sum_{d\mid n}d-\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d)\\
 &=2\sigma(n)-Y(n). \tag{1}
\end{aligned}
\]

Both \(\sigma\) and \(Y\) are multiplicative. More precisely, if \(m\) and \(n\) are coprime, then every divisor of \(mn\) has a unique expression \(ef\), where \(e\mid m\) and \(f\mid n\), and \(e\) and \(f\) are coprime. This divisor decomposition first gives
\[
\sigma(mn)=\sum_{e\mid m,\,f\mid n}ef
          =\left(\sum_{e\mid m}e\right)
           \left(\sum_{f\mid n}f\right)
          =\sigma(m)\sigma(n).
\]
Applying the same decomposition and the multiplicativity of \(\sigma\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
Y(mn)
 &=\sum_{e\mid m,\,f\mid n}\sigma(ef)\\
 &=\sum_{e\mid m,\,f\mid n}\sigma(e)\sigma(f)\\
 &=Y(m)Y(n). \tag{2}
\end{aligned}
\]

We use the integer
\[
N=2^{14}\cdot 4409\cdot 458009.
\]
The two odd numbers occurring here are prime. For completeness, this can be established by the following short collection of Lucas primality certificates.

We use this elementary form of the Lucas criterion: suppose the complete prime factorization of \(r-1\) is known, and there is an integer \(b\) such that
\[
b^{r-1}\equiv1\pmod r
\]
and, for every prime \(q\mid r-1\),
\[
\gcd\bigl(b^{(r-1)/q}-1,r\bigr)=1.
\]
Then \(r\) is prime. Indeed, if \(s\) is any prime divisor of \(r\), the multiplicative order of \(b\) modulo \(s\) divides \(r-1\). The gcd conditions say that this order does not divide \((r-1)/q\) for any prime divisor \(q\) of \(r-1\). Consequently the order contains every prime power occurring in \(r-1\), and hence equals \(r-1\). It also divides \(s-1\), so \(r-1\le s-1\), or \(r\le s\). Since \(s\mid r\), this forces \(s=r\), proving that \(r\) is prime.

Starting from the evident primes \(2,3,5\), the required factorizations and witnesses are as follows. In each row, the displayed witness \(b\) satisfies \(b^{r-1}\equiv1\pmod r\); for each distinct prime \(q\) shown in the factorization of \(r-1\), the table gives the residue of \(b^{(r-1)/q}\) modulo \(r\). The gcd of one less than each displayed residue with \(r\) is \(1\). These are direct modular-exponentiation and Euclidean-algorithm calculations.

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
r&r-1&b& q:\ b^{(r-1)/q}\bmod r\\ \hline
7&2\cdot3&3&2:6,\quad3:2\\
19&2\cdot3^2&2&2:18,\quad3:7\\
29&2^2\cdot7&2&2:28,\quad7:16\\
229&2^2\cdot3\cdot19&6&2:228,\quad3:134,\quad19:165\\
57251&2\cdot5^3\cdot229&2&2:57250,\quad5:55371,\quad229:48088\\
4409&2^3\cdot19\cdot29&3&2:4408,\quad19:209,\quad29:3965\\
458009&2^3\cdot57251&3&2:458008,\quad57251:6561
\end{array}
\]

For clarity, the accompanying gcd calculations are
\[
\begin{array}{c|l}
r&\gcd(\text{displayed residue}-1,r)\\ \hline
7&\gcd(5,7)=\gcd(1,7)=1\\
19&\gcd(17,19)=\gcd(6,19)=1\\
29&\gcd(27,29)=\gcd(15,29)=1\\
229&\gcd(227,229)=\gcd(133,229)=\gcd(164,229)=1\\
57251&\gcd(57249,57251)=\gcd(55370,57251)=\gcd(48087,57251)=1\\
4409&\gcd(4407,4409)=\gcd(208,4409)=\gcd(3964,4409)=1\\
458009&\gcd(458007,458009)=\gcd(6560,458009)=1.
\end{array}
\]
Thus the criterion proves successively that \(7,19,29,229,57251,4409\), and \(458009\) are prime. In particular, the three factors \(2^{14}\), \(4409\), and \(458009\) are pairwise coprime.

We now evaluate the two terms on the right side of (1). For a prime \(p\),
\[
\sigma(p)=1+p.
\]
Also, the only divisors of \(p\) are \(1\) and \(p\), so
\[
Y(p)=\sigma(1)+\sigma(p)=1+(1+p)=p+2. \tag{3}
\]
For the power of two,
\[
\sigma(2^{14})=\sum_{k=0}^{14}2^k=2^{15}-1=32767. \tag{4}
\]
Moreover, the divisors of \(2^{14}\) are \(2^j\) for \(0\le j\le14\), and
\(
\sigma(2^j)=1+2+\cdots+2^j=2^{j+1}-1.
\)
Consequently
\[
\begin{aligned}
Y(2^{14})
 &=\sum_{j=0}^{14}\sigma(2^j)\\
 &=\sum_{j=0}^{14}(2^{j+1}-1)\\
 &=\left(2+2^2+\cdots+2^{15}\right)-15\\
 &=(2^{16}-2)-15\\
 &=65519. \tag{5}
\end{aligned}
\]

For the two odd prime factors, (3) gives
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
\sigma(4409)=4410, &Y(4409)=4411,\\
\sigma(458009)=458010, &Y(458009)=458011.
\end{array} \tag{6}
\]
Using pairwise coprimality and multiplicativity, equations (2), (4), (5), and (6) now yield
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sigma(N)
 &=\sigma(2^{14})\sigma(4409)\sigma(458009)\\
 &=32767\cdot4410\cdot458010\\
 &=66{,}183{,}576{,}284{,}700, \tag{7}
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
Y(N)
 &=Y(2^{14})Y(4409)Y(458009)\\
 &=65519\cdot4411\cdot458011\\
 &=132{,}367{,}152{,}569{,}399. \tag{8}
\end{aligned}
\]
For reference, the intermediate products are
\[
32767\cdot4410=144{,}502{,}470,
\qquad
65519\cdot4411=289{,}004{,}309,
\]
from which the final products in (7) and (8) follow by ordinary integer multiplication.

Substituting (7) and (8) into (1), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(N)
 &=2\sigma(N)-Y(N)\\
 &=2\cdot66{,}183{,}576{,}284{,}700
   -132{,}367{,}152{,}569{,}399\\
 &=132{,}367{,}152{,}569{,}400
   -132{,}367{,}152{,}569{,}399\\
 &=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Finally,
\[
N=2^{14}\cdot4409\cdot458009
 =33{,}085{,}221{,}781{,}504,
\]
which is positive and is plainly neither \(1\) nor \(12\). Thus \(a(N)=1\) for a positive integer \(N\notin\{1,12\}\). This directly disproves the conjectured equivalence that \(a(n)=1\) holds if and only if \(n=1\) or \(n=12\).
